newsitem.title: FRANCE: French nuclear spy trial due soon - paper.
newsitem.headline: French nuclear spy trial due soon - paper.

text.p: A French nuclear physics engineer will go on trial soon before a special court charged with selling secrets on nuclear weapons testing to the Russians, the daily Le Figaro said on Saturday.

An investigating magistrate was quoted as describing the affair, in which Francis Temperville and a Russian agent were said to have kept in contact by dropping orange peel and rose petals, as France's biggest military espionage case since World War Two.

The newspaper published what it said were details of a four-year probe on Temperville, 39, who has been held in a Paris jail since 1992 when he was charged with handing over papers on testing at Mururoa Atoll in the South Pacific in 1979-91.
The Interior Ministry said at the time of his arrest that Temperville, who worked at the Atomic Energy Centre (CEA), had admitted having supplied information and documents to a Russian agent.
According to the probe, Temperville, described as affable and a jazz enthusiast, began giving private lessons to a foreigner know to him as Serge in 1987.
Over several years, Serge, whose real name was Sergei Smyrev and who was the second secretary at the Russian embassy, purchased some 6,000 documents from him, Le Figaro said.
"I was subjected to verbal pressure from Serge. He would tell me 'Francis, don't leave us, because we have the means to find you'," the newspaper quoted Temperville as testifying.
In September 1989 and April 1990, Temperville handed over documents marked "Vulcan. Military secret" which included studies on Mururoa blasts.

According to an expert consulted by the magistrate, these files "focus on only one aspect of the weapon...but they allow (the reader) to evaluate the technical level reached by France. They enable a country to improve its weapons".
Le Figaro said Temperville would simply photocopy documents in his secretary's office and walk out at the end of the working day with the files in a plastic bag.

He dropped orange peel by a telegraph post close to the Orsay swimming pool in central Paris if he had to get in touch urgently with Serge. Serge's tactic was to drop rose petals under one of the arches of the Pont d'Orsay bridge over the river Seine.
Justice sources have said that Temperville was betrayed by a KGB agent stationed in the Russian Embassy in Paris, Viktor Ochienko, who defected to Britain earlier in 1992.
Temperville, who risks a 15-year jail sentence, admitted receiving 160,000 francs ($32,000) but Ochienko claimed he had been paid two million francs ($400,000), the sources said.
Temperville's lawyers say he is not guilty of treason.

Didier Belot, one of Temperville's lawyers, told Le Figaro that his client "had sinned out of naivete. The sums he received were ridiculous and there was no ideology in his action. He was trapped and he could never go back."
"The CEA has also its share of responsibility in the case. The ease with which the documents could be misappropriated is unsettling," Belot added.
In October 1992, a month after Temperville's arrest, France expelled four Russian intelligence agents for obtaining secret documents on French nuclear weapons testing. The four were not named.
